claim: Tamoxifen treatment reduced PC-1 protein in mesenteric arteries of Pkd1 ecKO mice to approximately 66.7% of that in Pkd1fl/fl control mice.
source: Western blotting demonstrated that tamoxifen treatment reduced PC-1 protein in mesenteric arteries of Pkd1 ecKO mice to ~66.7% of that in Pkd1fl/fl control mice (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A-B demonstrating quantified protein reduction.

claim: Tamoxifen did not alter the expression of PC-2, SK3 channels, IK channels, TRPV4 channels, Piezo1 channels, eNOS, or GPR68 in arteries of Pkd1 ecKO mice.
source: In contrast, tamoxifen did not alter the expression of PC-2, small-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ (SK3) channels, intermediate-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ (IK) channels, TRP vanniloid 4 (TRPV4) channels, Piezo1 channels, endothelial NO synthase (eNOS), or G protein-coupled receptor 68 (GPR68) in arteries of Pkd1 ecKO mice (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1A-B showing no significant changes in these proteins.

claim: PC-1 labeling was absent in ECs of Pkd1 ecKO mouse mesenteric arteries imaged en face.
source: Immunofluorescence experiments demonstrated that PC-1 labeling was absent in ECs of Pkd1 ecKO mouse mesenteric arteries imaged en face (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Flow stimulates a transient increase in inward current of approximately -1.3 pA/pF in Pkd1fl/fl endothelial cells.
source: Flow stimulated an initial transient increase in inward current of ~–1.3 pA/pF (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Flow stimulates a sustained reduction in inward current that reaches steady state at approximately -0.97 pA/pF in Pkd1fl/fl endothelial cells.
source: This transient increase in inward current was followed by a sustained reduction in inward current that reached steady state at ~–0.97 pA/pF in Pkd1fl/fl cells (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: The flow-activated transient inward current in Pkd1 ecKO cells was approximately 15.4% of that in Pkd1fl/fl cells.
source: In contrast, the flow-activated transient inward current in Pkd1 ecKO cells was ~15.4% of that in Pkd1fl/fl cells (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data comparing Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd1fl/fl cells in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The sustained flow-mediated reduction in inward current in Pkd1 ecKO cells was approximately 42.2% of that in Pkd1fl/fl cells.
source: Similarly, the sustained flow-mediated reduction in inward current in Pkd1 ecKO cells was ~42.2% of that in Pkd1fl/fl cells (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data comparing Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd1fl/fl cells in Figure 1D and F.

claim: Removal of bath Ca2+ during flow increased inward current only approximately -0.2 pA/pF in Pkd1 ecKO cells, or approximately 7.1% of that in Pkd1fl/fl cells.
source: Ca2+ removal under flow increased inward current only ~–0.2 pA/pF in Pkd1 ecKO cells, or ~7.1% of that in Pkd1fl/fl cells (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data in Figure 1D and F showing differential responses to Ca2+ removal.

claim: Flow stimulates a PC-1-dependent biphasic response composed of an initial transient inward current followed by a sustained Ca2+-dependent reduction in inward current in endothelial cells.
source: These data demonstrate that flow stimulates a PC-1-dependent biphasic response composed of an initial transient inward current followed by a sustained Ca2+-dependent reduction in inward current in ECs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the patch-clamp electrophysiology data presented in Figure 1D-F.

claim: At 80 mmHg, intraluminal flow hyperpolarized Pkd1fl/fl arteries by approximately 10 mV.
source: At 80 mmHg, intraluminal flow hyperpolarized Pkd1fl/fl arteries by ~10 mV, but Pkd1 ecKO arteries by only ~2.6 mV, or ~27.1% of that in controls (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by membrane potential measurements shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: At 80 mmHg, intraluminal flow hyperpolarized Pkd1 ecKO arteries by only approximately 2.6 mV, or approximately 27.1% of that in controls.
source: At 80 mmHg, intraluminal flow hyperpolarized Pkd1fl/fl arteries by ~10 mV, but Pkd1 ecKO arteries by only ~2.6 mV, or ~27.1% of that in controls (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by membrane potential measurements shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: PC-1 expressed in endothelial cells contributes to flow-mediated arterial hyperpolarization.
source: These data suggest that PC-1 expressed in ECs contributes to flow-mediated arterial hyperpolarization.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from membrane potential measurements showing reduced hyperpolarization in Pkd1 ecKO arteries.

claim: In Pkd1 ecKO arteries, dilations to on-off flow were approximately 34.8% of those in Pkd1fl/fl arteries.
source: In Pkd1 ecKO arteries, dilations to on-off flow were ~34.8% of those in Pkd1fl/fl arteries (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ACh-induced vasodilation was similar in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1 ecKO arteries.
source: In contrast, ACh-induced vasodilation was similar in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1 ecKO arteries (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Flow-mediated dilation in Pkd1 ecKO arteries was attenuated over the entire shear-stress range to between approximately 38.0% and 50.0% of that in Pkd1fl/fl arteries.
source: Flow-mediated dilation in Pkd1 ecKO arteries was attenuated over the entire shear-stress range to between ~38.0% and 50.0% of that in Pkd1fl/fl arteries (Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data across different shear stress levels shown in Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Myogenic tone, depolarization (60 mM K+)-induced constriction and passive diameter were similar in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1 ecKO arteries.
source: Myogenic tone, depolarization (60 mM K+)-induced constriction and passive diameter were similar in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1 ecKO arteries (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-F).
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: A broad intravascular flow range activates PC-1 in endothelial cells to induce vasodilation.
source: These data indicate that a broad intravascular flow range activates PC-1 in ECs to induce vasodilation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from pressurized artery myography data showing PC-1-dependent vasodilation across multiple shear stress levels.

claim: PC-1 knockout reduced the L-NNA-sensitive component of flow-mediated dilation to approximately 21.6% of that in Pkd1fl/fl arteries.
source: PC-1 knockout reduced the L-NNA-, Tram-34-, and apamin-sensitive components of flow-mediated dilation to ~21.6%, 13.5%, and 18.6% of those in Pkd1fl/fl arteries, respectively (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data with pharmacological inhibitors shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: PC-1 knockout reduced the Tram-34-sensitive component of flow-mediated dilation to approximately 13.5% of that in Pkd1fl/fl arteries.
source: PC-1 knockout reduced the L-NNA-, Tram-34-, and apamin-sensitive components of flow-mediated dilation to ~21.6%, 13.5%, and 18.6% of those in Pkd1fl/fl arteries, respectively (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data with pharmacological inhibitors shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: PC-1 knockout reduced the apamin-sensitive component of flow-mediated dilation to approximately 18.6% of that in Pkd1fl/fl arteries.
source: PC-1 knockout reduced the L-NNA-, Tram-34-, and apamin-sensitive components of flow-mediated dilation to ~21.6%, 13.5%, and 18.6% of those in Pkd1fl/fl arteries, respectively (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data with pharmacological inhibitors shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: Flow stimulates PC-1-mediated dilation via NOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation in endothelial cells.
source: These data indicate that flow stimulates PC-1-mediated dilation via NOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation in ECs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from pharmacological inhibition experiments showing reduced flow-mediated dilation with L-NNA, Tram-34, and apamin in Pkd1 ecKO arteries.

claim: Intravascular flow increased p-eNOS (S1176) protein approximately 1.40-fold in Pkd1fl/fl arteries.
source: Western blotting experiments indicated that intravascular flow increased p-eNOS (S1176) protein ~1.40-fold in Pkd1fl/fl arteries, but did not alter p-eNOS in Pkd1 ecKO arteries (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing flow-induced eNOS phosphorylation in Figure 2I and J.

claim: Intravascular flow did not alter p-eNOS in Pkd1 ecKO arteries.
source: Western blotting experiments indicated that intravascular flow increased p-eNOS (S1176) protein ~1.40-fold in Pkd1fl/fl arteries, but did not alter p-eNOS in Pkd1 ecKO arteries (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing no change in eNOS phosphorylation in Pkd1 ecKO arteries in Figure 2I and J.

claim: Flow did not alter total eNOS in either Pkd1fl/fl or Pkd1 ecKO arteries.
source: In contrast, flow did not alter total eNOS in either genotype (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing no change in total eNOS protein in Figure 2I and J.

claim: Flow stimulates PC-1 in endothelial cells, leading to eNOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation, which produces vasodilation.
source: These data indicate that flow stimulates PC-1 in ECs, leading to eNOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation, which produces vasodilation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Western blot and pharmacological inhibition data showing PC-1-dependent activation of eNOS and K+ channels.

claim: Mean arterial pressure was approximately 89.9 mmHg in Pkd1fl/fl mice and approximately 109.6 mmHg in Pkd1 ecKO mice, or 21.9% higher.
source: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was ~89.9 mmHg in Pkd1fl/fl mice and ~109.6 mmHg in Pkd1 ecKO mice, or 21.9% higher (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Systolic and diastolic blood pressures were higher in Pkd1 ecKO mice.
source: Underlying this increase in MAP were higher systolic and diastolic blood pressures in Pkd1 ecKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Heart rate and activity were similar in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1 ecKO mice.
source: In contrast, heart rate and activity were similar in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1 ecKO mice, as were proximal tubule diameter and glomerular surface area measured in hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained kidney sections (Figure 3C–F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by telemetric measurements and histological analysis shown in Figure 3C-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Proximal tubule diameter and glomerular surface area were similar in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1 ecKO mice.
source: In contrast, heart rate and activity were similar in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd1 ecKO mice, as were proximal tubule diameter and glomerular surface area measured in hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained kidney sections (Figure 3C–F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of kidney sections shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Flow stimulates PC-1 in endothelial cells, leading to vasodilation and a reduction in systemic blood pressure.
source: These results suggest that flow stimulates PC-1 in ECs, leading to vasodilation and a reduction in systemic blood pressure.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from blood pressure measurements showing elevated pressure in Pkd1 ecKO mice.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 coimmunoprecipitate in mesenteric artery lysate.
source: PC-1 and PC-2 coimmunoprecipitated in mesenteric artery lysate, suggesting they coassemble (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Immunofluorescence energy transfer microscopy generated mean N-FRET of approximately 24.3% in endothelial cells of Pkd1fl/fl mice.
source: Immunofluorescence energy transfer (immunoFRET) microscopy using Alexa Fluor 546 and Alexa Fluor 488-tagged secondary antibodies bound to PC-1 and PC-2 primary antibodies, respectively, generated mean N-FRET of ~24.3% in ECs of Pkd1fl/fl mice (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunoFRET microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: N-FRET was only approximately 1.3% and 0.9% in Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO endothelial cells, respectively.
source: In contrast, N-FRET was only ~1.3% and 0.9% in Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO ECs, respectively, when using the same labeling procedure (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by immunoFRET microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 locate in close spatial proximity in endothelial cells.
source: Given that the Förster coefficient of the Alexa Fluor pair used is ∼6.3 nm, these data suggest PC-1 and PC-2 locate in close spatial proximity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from immunoFRET data showing high N-FRET values in Pkd1fl/fl cells and the known Förster coefficient.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 colocalize in endothelial cells as measured by Pearson's and Mander's coefficients.
source: Analysis of these data using both Pearson's and Mander's coefficients also indicated that PC-1 and PC-2 colocalize in ECs (Figure 4E and G; Bolte and Cordelières, 2006).
evidence: Supported by Lattice-SIM imaging and colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4E and G.

claim: Discrete clusters of PC-1 and PC-2 were observed in the plasma membrane of Pkd1fl/fl endothelial cells.
source: Discrete clusters of PC-1 and PC-2 were observed in the plasma membrane of Pkd1fl/fl ECs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 clusters exhibited similar densities in Pkd1fl/fl endothelial cells.
source: PC-1 and PC-2 clusters exhibited similar densities (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The mean sizes of individual PC-1 and PC-2 clusters were approximately 3702.5 and 2157.1 nm2, respectively.
source: The sizes (areas) of individual PC-1 and PC-2 clusters were exponentially distributed, with means of ~3702.5 and 2157.1 nm2, respectively (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and cluster size analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: PC-2 clusters were smaller than PC-1 clusters in Pkd1fl/fl endothelial cells.
source: PC-2 clusters were smaller than PC-1 clusters (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and cluster size analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The mean PC-1 to PC-2 intercentroid distance was approximately 126.8 nm in Pkd1fl/fl cells.
source: The mean PC-1 to PC-2 intercentroid distance was ~126.8 nm in Pkd1fl/fl cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and nearest-neighbor analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Approximately 27.0% of PC-1 clusters overlapped with a PC-2 cluster in Pkd1fl/fl endothelial cells.
source: Approximately 27.0% of PC-1 clusters overlapped with a PC-2 cluster and ~26.6% of PC-2 clusters overlapped with a PC-1 cluster in Pkd1fl/fl ECs (Figure 5E and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and overlap analysis shown in Figure 5E-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Approximately 26.6% of PC-2 clusters overlapped with a PC-1 cluster in Pkd1fl/fl endothelial cells.
source: Approximately 27.0% of PC-1 clusters overlapped with a PC-2 cluster and ~26.6% of PC-2 clusters overlapped with a PC-1 cluster in Pkd1fl/fl ECs (Figure 5E and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and overlap analysis shown in Figure 5E-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: When experimental data were randomized using Costes' simulation algorithm, PC-1 to PC-2 and PC-2 to PC-1 overlap were only approximately 7.8% and 7.2%, respectively, in Pkd1fl/fl cells.
source: When experimental data were randomized using Costes' simulation algorithm (Bolte and Cordelières, 2006), PC-1 to PC-2 and PC-2 to PC-1 overlap were only ~7.8% and 7.2%, respectively, in Pkd1fl/fl cells (Figure 5E and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data with Costes' randomization analysis shown in Figure 5E-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Flow did not alter PC-1 or PC-2 cluster density, PC-1 or PC-2 cluster size, the distance between PC-1 and PC-2 centroids, or their overlap.
source: Flow did not alter PC-1 or PC-2 cluster density, PC-1 or PC-2 cluster size, the distance between PC-1 and PC-2 centroids, or their overlap (Figure 5B–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data comparing static and flow conditions shown in Figure 5B-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: In Pkd1 ecKO cells, the densities of PC-1 and PC-2 clusters were approximately 15.7% and 18.3%, respectively, of those in endothelial cells of Pkd1fl/fl mice.
source: In Pkd1 ecKO cells, the densities of PC-1 and PC-2 clusters were far lower, at ~15.7% and 18.3%, respectively, of those in ECs of Pkd1fl/fl mice (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data comparing Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd1fl/fl cells shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The mean sizes of PC-1 and PC-2 clusters in Pkd1 ecKO endothelial cells were approximately 17.7% and 28.3% of those, respectively, in Pkd1fl/fl cells.
source: The mean sizes of PC-1 and PC-2 clusters in Pkd1 ecKO ECs were ~17.7% and 28.3% of those, respectively, in Pkd1fl/fl cells (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and cluster size analysis comparing Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd1fl/fl cells shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The mean PC-1 to PC-2 distance was approximately 5.79-fold larger in Pkd1 ecKO than Pkd1fl/fl cells.
source: The mean PC-1 to PC-2 distance was ~5.79-fold larger in Pkd1 ecKO than Pkd1fl/fl cells (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and nearest-neighbor analysis comparing Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd1fl/fl cells shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Only approximately 1.2% of PC-1 clusters overlapped with a PC-2 cluster in Pkd1 ecKO cells.
source: Furthermore, only ~1.2% of PC-1 clusters overlapped with a PC-2 cluster in Pkd1 ecKO cells, with similar results for PC-2 to PC-1 overlap (Figure 5E and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and overlap analysis in Pkd1 ecKO cells shown in Figure 5E-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 surface protein clusters are colocalized in endothelial cells.
source: These data indicate that: (1) PC-1 and PC-2 surface protein clusters are colocalized in ECs, (2) PC-1 or PC-2 knockout inhibits surface expression of both PC-1 and PC-2 proteins, and (3) fluorescent clusters in Pkd1 ecKO cells are likely due to nonspecific labeling by secondary antibodies.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SMLM-TIRF imaging data showing cluster colocalization and interdependency.

claim: PC-1 or PC-2 knockout inhibits surface expression of both PC-1 and PC-2 proteins.
source: These data indicate that: (1) PC-1 and PC-2 surface protein clusters are colocalized in ECs, (2) PC-1 or PC-2 knockout inhibits surface expression of both PC-1 and PC-2 proteins, and (3) fluorescent clusters in Pkd1 ecKO cells are likely due to nonspecific labeling by secondary antibodies.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SMLM-TIRF imaging data showing reduced cluster density and size in knockout cells.

claim: Fluorescent clusters in Pkd1 ecKO cells are likely due to nonspecific labeling by secondary antibodies.
source: These data indicate that: (1) PC-1 and PC-2 surface protein clusters are colocalized in ECs, (2) PC-1 or PC-2 knockout inhibits surface expression of both PC-1 and PC-2 proteins, and (3) fluorescent clusters in Pkd1 ecKO cells are likely due to nonspecific labeling by secondary antibodies.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SMLM-TIRF imaging data showing minimal clusters in knockout cells.

claim: Tamoxifen-treatment reduced PC-1 and PC-2 proteins in mesenteric arteries of Pkd1fl/fl/Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5(PAC)-CreERT2 mice to approximately 60.9% and 66.1%, respectively, of those in Pkd1fl/fl/Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Tamoxifen-treatment reduced PC-1 and PC-2 proteins in mesenteric arteries of Pkd1fl/fl/Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5(PAC)-CreERT2 mice to ~60.9% and 66.1%, respectively, of those in Pkd1fl/fl/Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 6A and B, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: eNOS was similar in Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO arteries and Pkd1fl/fl/Pkd2fl/fl arteries.
source: In contrast, eNOS was similar in Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO arteries and Pkd1fl/fl/Pkd2fl/fl arteries (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: In Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO mouse arteries, mean flow-mediated vasodilation at 15 and 23 dyn/cm2 were approximately 38.8% and 50.4% of those in Pkd1fl/fl/Pkd2fl/fl arteries, respectively.
source: In Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO mouse arteries, mean flow-mediated vasodilation at 15 and 23 dyn/cm2 were ~38.8% and 50.4% of those in Pkd1fl/fl/Pkd2fl/fl arteries, respectively (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: 60 mM K+-induced constriction, myogenic tone, dilations to ACh, or sodium nitroprusside (SNP), and passive diameter were similar in Pkd1fl/fl/Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO arteries.
source: In contrast, 60 mM K+-induced constriction, myogenic tone, dilations to ACh, or sodium nitroprusside (SNP), a NO donor, and passive diameter were similar in Pkd1fl/fl/Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO arteries (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-E).
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: Flow reversibly stimulated sustained inward ICats that were of similar amplitude in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl endothelial cells.
source: At a steady-state holding potential of –60 mV, flow reversibly stimulated sustained inward ICats that were of similar amplitude in Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl ECs (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: In Pkd1 ecKO endothelial cells, mean flow-activated ICat was approximately 23.3% of that in Pkd1fl/fl controls.
source: In Pkd1 ecKO ECs, mean flow-activated ICat was ~23.3% of that in Pkd1fl/fl controls (Figure 6E and G).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6E and G.

claim: Flow-activated ICat in Pkd2 ecKO cells was approximately 22.5% of that in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: Flow-activated ICat in Pkd2 ecKO cells was similarly smaller, at ~22.5% of that in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 6E and G).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6E and G.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 similarly contribute to flow-activated ICat in endothelial cells.
source: These data indicate that PC-1 and PC-2 similarly contribute to flow-activated ICat in ECs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from patch-clamp electrophysiology data showing similar reductions in ICat in both Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO cells.

claim: Intracellular introduction via the pipette solution of either the PC-1 or PC-2 coiled-coil domain peptide similarly reduced flow-activated ICats to between approximately 30.1% and 29% of control currents in both Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl endothelial cells.
source: Intracellular introduction via the pipette solution of either the PC-1 or PC-2 coiled-coil domain peptide similarly reduced flow-activated ICats to between ~30.1% and 29% of control currents in both Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl ECs (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data with interference peptides shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: Scrambled PC-1 and PC-2 peptides did not alter flow-activated ICats.
source: In contrast, scrambled PC-1 and PC-2 peptides did not alter flow-activated ICats (Figure 6G; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data with scrambled peptides shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 are interdependent for flow to activate ICat in endothelial cells.
source: These data indicate that PC-1 and PC-2 are interdependent for flow to activate ICat in ECs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from patch-clamp electrophysiology data showing similar effects of PC-1 and PC-2 knockout and interference peptides.

claim: Physical coupling of PC-1 and PC-2 C-termini is necessary for flow to activate ICat.
source: Data also suggest that physical coupling of PC-1 and PC-2 C-termini is necessary for flow to activate ICat.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from patch-clamp electrophysiology data showing that coiled-coil domain peptides inhibit flow-activated ICat.

claim: Flow stimulates PC-1-dependent cation currents in endothelial cells that induce arterial hyperpolarization, vasodilation, and a reduction in blood pressure.
source: Our data show that flow stimulates PC-1-dependent cation currents in ECs that induce arterial hyperpolarization, vasodilation, and a reduction in blood pressure.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including patch-clamp, myography, and blood pressure measurements.

claim: PC-1-dependent vasodilation occurs over the entire functional shear stress range due to eNOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation.
source: PC-1-dependent vasodilation occurs over the entire functional shear stress range due to eNOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from myography experiments across different shear stress levels and pharmacological inhibition studies.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 proteins coassemble and their surface clusters colocalize.
source: PC-1 and PC-2 proteins coassemble and their surface clusters colocalize.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from co-immunoprecipitation, immunoFRET, and SMLM-TIRF imaging data.

claim: Knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 abolishes surface expression of both proteins.
source: Knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 abolishes surface expression of both proteins.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from SMLM-TIRF imaging data showing reduced cluster density and size in knockout cells.

claim: Flow activates a PC-1- and PC-2-dependent ICat that is inhibited by peptides corresponding to the C-terminus coiled-coil domains on either polycystin protein.
source: Flow activates a PC-1- and PC-2-dependent ICat that is inhibited by peptides corresponding to the C-terminus coiled-coil domains on either polycystin protein.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from patch-clamp electrophysiology data with interference peptides.

claim: PC-1 regulates arterial contractility by forming an interdependent complex with PC-2 in endothelial cells.
source: These data demonstrate that PC-1 regulates arterial contractility by forming an interdependent complex with PC-2 in ECs.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all experimental data showing functional and structural interdependence of PC-1 and PC-2.

claim: Flow stimulates plasma membrane-localized PC-1/PC-2 clusters, leading to eNOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation, vasodilation, and a reduction in blood pressure.
source: Flow stimulates plasma membrane-localized PC-1/PC-2 clusters, leading to eNOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation, vasodilation, and a reduction in blood pressure.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all experimental data including imaging, electrophysiology, myography, and blood pressure measurements.

claim: PC-1 is a receptor-like transmembrane protein encoded by the Pkd1 gene.
source: Polycystin-1 (PC-1, PKD1) is a receptor-like transmembrane protein encoded by the Pkd1 gene (Hughes et al., 1995).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Hughes et al., 1995.

claim: PC-1 is expressed in various cell types, including endothelial cells.
source: PC-1 is expressed in various cell types, including ECs, and is predicted to form eleven transmembrane helices, an extracellular N-terminus, and an intracellular C-terminus (Hughes et al., 1995; Boulter et al., 2001; Bulley et al., 2018; MacKay et al., 2020; Burn et al., 1995; Qian et al., 2002).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: PC-1 is predicted to form eleven transmembrane helices, an extracellular N-terminus, and an intracellular C-terminus.
source: PC-1 is expressed in various cell types, including ECs, and is predicted to form eleven transmembrane helices, an extracellular N-terminus, and an intracellular C-terminus (Hughes et al., 1995; Boulter et al., 2001; Bulley et al., 2018; MacKay et al., 2020; Burn et al., 1995; Qian et al., 2002).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: The PC-1 N-terminus is large (>3000 amino acid residues) and contains multiple putative adhesion- and ligand-binding sites.
source: The PC-1 N-terminus is large (>3000 amino acid residues) and contains multiple putative adhesion- and ligand-binding sites (Hughes et al., 1995; Burn et al., 1995; Qian et al., 2002; Hardy and Tsiokas, 2020; Zhou, 2009; Nauli et al., 2003).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: PC-1 is proposed to act as a mechanical sensor and ligand-receptor.
source: As such, PC-1 is proposed to act as a mechanical sensor and ligand-receptor, although stimuli that activate PC-1 and its functional significance are unclear.
evidence: Established hypothesis in the field, though the authors note uncertainty about activation mechanisms.

claim: PC-2 is a member of the transient receptor potential (TRP) channel family and is also termed TRP polycystin 1 (TRPP1).
source: PC-2 is a member of the transient receptor potential (TRP) channel family and is also termed TRP polycystin 1 (TRPP1) (Earley and Brayden, 2015).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Earley and Brayden, 2015.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 have been proposed to signal through independent and interdependent mechanisms.
source: PC-1 and PC-2 have been proposed to signal through independent and interdependent mechanisms, with much of this knowledge derived from experiments studying recombinant proteins and cultured cells (Hardy and Tsiokas, 2020; Brill and Ehrlich, 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Hardy and Tsiokas, 2020 and Brill and Ehrlich, 2020.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 exhibit distinct developmental and expression profiles in different kidney cell types.
source: Supporting their independence, PC-1 and PC-2 exhibit distinct developmental and expression profiles in different kidney cell types (Foggensteiner et al., 2000).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Foggensteiner et al., 2000.

claim: PC-2 channels do not require PC-1 to traffic to primary cilia and generate currents in primary-cultured kidney collecting duct cells.
source: PC-2 channels do not require PC-1 to traffic to primary cilia and generate currents in primary-cultured kidney collecting duct cells (Liu et al., 2018; Arif Pavel et al., 2016).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Liu et al., 2018 and Arif Pavel et al., 2016.

claim: PC-1 is proposed to act as an atypical G protein-coupled receptor.
source: PC-1 is also proposed to act as an atypical G protein-coupled receptor (Parnell et al., 1998).
evidence: Established hypothesis cited from Parnell et al., 1998.

claim: C- and N-terminus-deficient PC-2 can alone form a homotetrameric ion channel with each subunit containing six transmembrane domains.
source: In addition, C- and N-terminus-deficient PC-2 can alone form a homotetrameric ion channel with each subunit containing six transmembrane domains, when visualized using cryo-EM (Shen et al., 2016; Grieben et al., 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Shen et al., 2016 and Grieben et al., 2017.

claim: Mutations in either Pkd1 or Pkd2 result in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the most prevalent monogenic disorder in humans.
source: Evidence supporting PC-1 and PC-2 interdependency includes that mutations in either Pkd1 or Pkd2 result in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the most prevalent monogenic disorder in humans (Rossetti et al., 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Rossetti et al., 2007.

claim: ADPKD is typically characterized by the appearance of renal cysts, but patients can develop hypertension before any kidney dysfunction.
source: ADPKD is typically characterized by the appearance of renal cysts, but patients can develop hypertension before any kidney dysfunction and cardiovascular disease is the leading (~50%) cause of death in patients (Valero et al., 1999; Martinez-Vea et al., 2004; Torres et al., 2007; Gabow, 1990; Bergmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: Cardiovascular disease is the leading (~50%) cause of death in ADPKD patients.
source: ADPKD is typically characterized by the appearance of renal cysts, but patients can develop hypertension before any kidney dysfunction and cardiovascular disease is the leading (~50%) cause of death in patients (Valero et al., 1999; Martinez-Vea et al., 2004; Torres et al., 2007; Gabow, 1990; Bergmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 can exist in a protein complex.
source: Experiments studying recombinant proteins and cultured kidney cell lines have provided evidence that PC-1 and PC-2 can exist in a protein complex (Nauli et al., 2003; Su et al., 2018; Qian et al., 1997; Newby et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2009; Hanaoka et al., 2000; Delmas et al., 2004).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: Several domains in PC-1 and PC-2 may physically interact, including their C-terminus coiled-coils.
source: Several domains in PC-1 and PC-2 may physically interact, including their C-terminus coiled-coils (Su et al., 2018; Qian et al., 1997; Zhu et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2009; Tsiokas et al., 1997).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: The structure of a PC-1/PC-2 heterotetrameric complex, which forms in a 1:3 stoichiometry, has been resolved using cryo-EM.
source: The structure of a PC-1/PC-2 heterotetrameric complex, which forms in a 1:3 stoichiometry, has also been resolved using cryo-EM (Su et al., 2018).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Su et al., 2018.

claim: Blood vessels are lined by endothelial cells, which regulate several physiological functions, including contractility, to control regional organ flow and systemic pressure.
source: Blood vessels are lined by endothelial cells (ECs), which regulate several physiological functions, including contractility, to control regional organ flow and systemic pressure.
evidence: Established knowledge in vascular biology.

claim: Endothelial cells can release several diffusible factors, including nitric oxide (NO), which relaxes arterial smooth muscle cells, leading to vasodilation.
source: ECs can release several diffusible factors, including nitric oxide (NO), which relaxes arterial smooth muscle cells, leading to vasodilation (Vane, 1993).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Vane, 1993.

claim: Endothelial cells electrically couple to smooth muscle cells and directly modulate their membrane potential to modify arterial contractility.
source: ECs also electrically couple to smooth muscle cells and directly modulate their membrane potential to modify arterial contractility (Garland et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Garland et al., 2011.

claim: Flow activates SK and inwardly rectifying K+ (Kir) channels to induce vasodilation.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that flow activates SK and inwardly rectifying K+ (Kir) channels to induce vasodilation (Ahn et al., 2017; Brähler et al., 2009; Taylor et al., 2003).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: Kir2.1 activation contributes to eNOS phosphorylation, but not to SK channel activation.
source: Kir2.1 activation was shown to contribute to eNOS phosphorylation, but not to SK channel activation (Ahn et al., 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Ahn et al., 2017.

claim: Virtually all vertebrate cells possess at least one primary cilia.
source: Virtually all vertebrate cells possess at least one primary cilia, a tiny (~0.2–0.5 µm width, 1–12 µm length) immotile organelle electrically distinct from the cell body (Kleene and Van Houten, 2014; Delling et al., 2013; DeCaen et al., 2013).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: Primary cilia generate compartmentalized signaling and maintain an intracellular Ca2+ concentration distinct from the cell soma.
source: Cilia generate compartmentalized signaling and maintain an intracellular Ca2+ concentration distinct from the cell soma (Kleene and Van Houten, 2014; Delling et al., 2013; DeCaen et al., 2013).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: Primary cilia act as flow sensors in the embryonic node and in kidney collecting duct cells.
source: Primary cilia act as flow sensors in the embryonic node and in kidney collecting duct cells (Yoshiba et al., 2012; Praetorius and Spring, 2003).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Yoshiba et al., 2012 and Praetorius and Spring, 2003.

claim: Flow does not activate Ca2+ influx in primary cilia of cultured kidney epithelial cells, kidney thick ascending tubules, embryonic node crown cells, or in the kinocilia of inner ear hair cells.
source: In contrast, flow does not activate Ca2+ influx in primary cilia of cultured kidney epithelial cells, kidney thick ascending tubules, embryonic node crown cells, or in the kinocilia of inner ear hair cells (Delling et al., 2016).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Delling et al., 2016.

claim: Flow stimulates a cytoplasmic Ca2+ signal in the cell body that propagates to cilia to elevate intraciliary Ca2+ concentration.
source: Instead, flow stimulates a cytoplasmic Ca2+ signal in the cell body that propagates to cilia to elevate intraciliary Ca2+ concentration (Delling et al., 2016).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Delling et al., 2016.

claim: Flow stimulated plasma membrane cation currents, indicating that flow-sensing takes place in the cell body of endothelial cells.
source: Here, flow stimulated plasma membrane cation currents, indicating that flow-sensing takes place in the cell body of ECs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from patch-clamp electrophysiology data showing flow-activated currents in the cell body.

claim: Ciliary localization of PC-2 is necessary for flow-sensing in perinodal crown cells and left-right symmetry in mouse embryos.
source: Ciliary localization of PC-2 is necessary for flow-sensing in perinodal crown cells and left-right symmetry in mouse embryos (Yoshiba et al., 2012).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Yoshiba et al., 2012.

claim: A physical interaction between PC-1 and PC-2 is essential for these proteins to traffic to the cell surface and generate plasma membrane currents.
source: In contrast, other studies demonstrated that a physical interaction between PC-1 and PC-2 is essential for these proteins to traffic to the cell surface and generate plasma membrane currents (Su et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2009; Hanaoka et al., 2000; Delmas et al., 2004; Chapin et al., 2010; Gainullin et al., 2015; Ha et al., 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: It was essential to include an IgҠ-chain secretion sequence into recombinant PC-1 to induce its trafficking and that of associated PC-2 to the plasma membrane in HEK293 cells.
source: It was essential to include an IgҠ-chain secretion sequence into recombinant PC-1 to induce its trafficking and that of associated PC-2 to the plasma membrane in HEK293 cells (Ha et al., 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Ha et al., 2020.

claim: When PC-1 and PC-2 are both expressed, they readily traffic to the plasma membrane in endothelial cells.
source: We show that when PC-1 and PC-2 are both expressed, they readily traffic to the plasma membrane in ECs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SMLM-TIRF imaging data showing surface clusters of PC-1 and PC-2.

claim: Knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 does not alter the amount of the other polycystin protein.
source: Knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 does not alter the amount of the other polycystin protein, suggesting that the expression of each polycystin is not influenced by that of the other.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Western blot data showing no change in total protein levels of PC-2 in Pkd1 ecKO mice and vice versa.

claim: PC-1 or PC-2 knockout prevents surface localization of the other polycystin protein, leading to its intracellular retention.
source: In contrast, PC-1 or PC-2 knockout prevents surface localization of the other polycystin protein, leading to its intracellular retention, as can be seen in SMLM and immunofluorescence imaging experiments.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SMLM-TIRF and immunofluorescence imaging data showing reduced surface clusters in knockout cells.

claim: Flow activates a heteromeric PC-1/PC-2 complex in the plasma membrane.
source: Flow did not alter the properties of surface PC-1 or PC-2 clusters, or their intercluster distance or overlap, suggesting that flow activates a heteromeric PC-1/PC-2 complex in the plasma membrane.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SMLM-TIRF imaging data showing no change in cluster properties under flow.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 did not generate currents in the plasma membrane of renal collecting duct cells or following heterologous expression in cell lines.
source: PC-1 and PC-2 did not generate currents in the plasma membrane of renal collecting duct cells or following heterologous expression in cell lines (Liu et al., 2018; Arif Pavel et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2016; Hanaoka et al., 2000; Delmas et al., 2004; DeCaen et al., 2013).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: Knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 did not alter plasma membrane currents in inner medullary collecting duct (pIMCD) epithelial cells.
source: Knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 also did not alter plasma membrane currents in inner medullary collecting duct (pIMCD) epithelial cells (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Liu et al., 2018.

claim: Plasma membrane PC-1/PC-2 channels are silent but can be measured when a gain-of-function mutation (F604P) is introduced into PC-2.
source: Recently, it was demonstrated that plasma membrane PC-1/PC-2 channels are silent but can be measured when a gain-of-function mutation (F604P) is introduced into PC-2 (Ha et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Ha et al., 2020 and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: In the absence of flow, surface PC-1/PC-2 channels generate little current in endothelial cells.
source: We show that in the absence of flow, surface PC-1/PC-2 channels generate little current in ECs (MacKay et al., 2020).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from patch-clamp electrophysiology data cited from MacKay et al., 2020.

claim: Flow-mediated intracellular Ca2+ elevations and NO production were attenuated in cultured embryonic aortic endothelial cells from Pkd1 and Tg737orpk/orpk global knockout mice.
source: Flow-mediated intracellular Ca2+ elevations and NO production were attenuated in cultured embryonic aortic ECs from Pkd1 and Tg737orpk/orpk global knockout mice (Nauli et al., 2008).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Nauli et al., 2008.

claim: PC-1 located in cilia is proposed to be a flow sensor in embryonic endothelial cells.
source: As Tg737orpk/orpk global knockout mice have shorter cilia or no cilia, the authors proposed that PC-1 located in cilia is a flow sensor in embryonic ECs (Nauli et al., 2008).
evidence: Hypothesis proposed by Nauli et al., 2008.

claim: Flow did not elicit Ca2+ signaling in primary cilia and homomeric PC-2 channels did not require PC-1 in primary cilia of pIMCD epithelial cells.
source: In contrast, more recent studies have demonstrated that flow did not elicit Ca2+ signaling in primary cilia and homomeric PC-2 channels did not require PC-1 in primary cilia of pIMCD epithelial cells (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Liu et al., 2018.

claim: Flow activates PC-1/PC-2-dependent cation currents in the plasma membrane of endothelial cells.
source: Our data support the conclusion that flow activates PC-1/PC-2-dependent cation currents in the plasma membrane of ECs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from patch-clamp electrophysiology data showing flow-activated currents dependent on PC-1 and PC-2.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 couple via their C-terminal coiled-coils.
source: Several groups have demonstrated that PC-1 and PC-2 couple via their C-terminal coiled-coils (Qian et al., 1997; Zhu et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2009; Tsiokas et al., 1997).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: Recombinant PC-1 and PC-2 lacking coiled-coils can interact via N-terminal loops.
source: Recombinant PC-1 and PC-2 lacking coiled-coils can also interact via N-terminal loops (Babich et al., 2004; Feng et al., 2008).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Babich et al., 2004 and Feng et al., 2008.

claim: A region between TM6 and TM11 of PC-1 interdigitates with PC-2.
source: The structure of a PC-1/PC-2 heterotetramer resolved using cryo-EM indicated that a region between TM6 and TM11 of PC-1 interdigitates with PC-2 (Su et al., 2018).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Su et al., 2018.

claim: PC-1 is proposed to act both as a dominant-negative subunit in PC-1/PC-2 channels and to increase Ca2+ permeability over that in PC-2 homotetramers.
source: PC-1 is proposed to act both as a dominant-negative subunit in PC-1/PC-2 channels and to increase Ca2+ permeability over that in PC-2 homotetramers (Su et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Established hypothesis cited from Su et al., 2018 and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Flow stimulates the physical coupling of the coiled-coil domains in PC-1/PC-2 to activate current.
source: Our data suggest that flow stimulates the physical coupling of the coiled-coil domains in PC-1/PC-2 to activate current.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from patch-clamp electrophysiology data showing that coiled-coil domain peptides inhibit flow-activated currents.

claim: The interference peptides may uncouple constitutively bound coiled coils in PC-1/PC-2 heteromers, thereby preventing current activation by flow.
source: Alternatively, the interference peptides may uncouple constitutively bound coiled coils in PC-1/PC-2 heteromers, thereby preventing current activation by flow.
evidence: Alternative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: PC-1 has been proposed to act as an atypical G protein due to the presence of a G protein-binding domain located in the C-terminus.
source: PC-1 has been proposed to act as an atypical G protein due to the presence of a G protein-binding domain located in the C-terminus (Parnell et al., 1998).
evidence: Established hypothesis cited from Parnell et al., 1998.

claim: Homomeric PC-2 is a K+- and Na+-permeant channel with low Ca2+ permeability.
source: Although homomeric PC-2 is a K+- and Na+-permeant channel with low Ca2+ permeability, heteromeric assembly of PC-2 with PC-1 increases Ca2+ permeability and reduces block by external Ca2+, supporting this concept (Liu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Liu et al., 2018 and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Heteromeric assembly of PC-2 with PC-1 increases Ca2+ permeability and reduces block by external Ca2+.
source: Although homomeric PC-2 is a K+- and Na+-permeant channel with low Ca2+ permeability, heteromeric assembly of PC-2 with PC-1 increases Ca2+ permeability and reduces block by external Ca2+, supporting this concept (Liu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Liu et al., 2018 and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: PC-2-containing channels have been suggested to require TRPM3 in primary cilia of cultured renal epithelial cells.
source: For example, PC-2-containing channels have been suggested to require TRPM3 in primary cilia of cultured renal epithelial cells (Kleene et al., 2019).
evidence: Established hypothesis cited from Kleene et al., 2019.

claim: PC-1/PC-2 channels in endothelial cells may contain other TRP subunits.
source: Thus, PC-1/PC-2 channels in ECs may contain other TRP subunits.
evidence: Speculation based on knowledge of PC-2 interactions with other TRP channels.

claim: The C-type lectin domain located in the PC-1 N-terminus activates recombinant PC-1/PC-2 channels.
source: Recent evidence indicates that the C-type lectin domain located in the PC-1 N-terminus activates recombinant PC-1/PC-2 channels, providing one possible activation mechanism for flow (Ha et al., 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Ha et al., 2020.

claim: Other mechanosensitive proteins, such as Piezo1 and GPR68, may stimulate PC-1/PC-2-dependent currents in endothelial cells.
source: Other mechanosensitive proteins, such as Piezo1 and GPR68, may also stimulate PC-1/PC-2-dependent currents in ECs (Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation based on knowledge of other mechanosensitive proteins cited from Xu et al., 2018 and Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Hypertension occurs prior to loss of kidney function in more than 60% of ADPKD patients, with the average age of onset between 30 and 34 years of age.
source: Hypertension occurs prior to loss of kidney function in more than 60% of patients, with the average age of onset between 30 and 34 years of age (Chapman et al., 2010).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Chapman et al., 2010.

claim: Hypertension and cardiovascular disease in ADPKD patients may involve altered PC-1/PC-2 function in endothelial cells.
source: Our study raises the possibility that hypertension and cardiovascular disease in ADPKD patients may involve altered PC-1/PC-2 function in ECs.
evidence: Speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: Human ADPKD patients exhibit loss of NO release and a reduction in endothelium-dependent dilation during increased blood flow.
source: Consistent with our data, human ADPKD patients exhibit loss of NO release and a reduction in endothelium-dependent dilation during increased blood flow (MacKay et al., 2020; Lorthioir et al., 2015).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from MacKay et al., 2020 and Lorthioir et al., 2015.

claim: Hypertension in humans is associated with endothelial dysfunction and attenuated flow-mediated dilation.
source: Hypertension in humans is also associated with endothelial dysfunction and attenuated flow-mediated dilation (Antony et al., 1995).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Antony et al., 1995.

claim: Hypertension may be associated with dysfunctional PC-1/PC-2 signaling in endothelial cells.
source: Conceivably, hypertension may also be associated with dysfunctional PC-1/PC-2 signaling in ECs.
evidence: Speculation based on the study's findings and known associations between hypertension and endothelial dysfunction.

claim: Phosphorylation of eNOS at serine 1176 (p-eNOS (S1176)) leads to its activation.
source: Phosphorylation of eNOS at serine 1176 (p-eNOS (S1176)) leads to its activation (Fulton et al., 1999; Dimmeler et al., 1999).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Fulton et al., 1999 and Dimmeler et al., 1999.

claim: The localization precision of the Alexa Fluor 488 and Alexa Fluor 647 fluorophores on secondary antibodies used for SMLM-TIRF were 29.6±0.6 (n=53) and 24.6±0.7 (n=45) nm, respectively, when imaged in endothelial cells.
source: Localization precision of the Alexa Fluor 488 and Alexa Fluor 647 fluorophores on secondary antibodies that were used for SMLM-TIRF were 29.6±0.6 (n=53) and 24.6±0.7 (n=45) nm, respectively, when imaged in ECs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by localization precision measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The sizes (areas) of individual PC-1 and PC-2 clusters were exponentially distributed.
source: The sizes (areas) of individual PC-1 and PC-2 clusters were exponentially distributed, with means of ~3702.5 and 2157.1 nm2, respectively (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and cluster size distribution analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The distance between the center of each PC-1 cluster and that of its nearest PC-2 neighbor was exponentially distributed.
source: Histograms were constructed that contained the distance between the center of each PC-1 cluster and that of its nearest PC-2 neighbor. These data were exponentially distributed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and nearest-neighbor distance distribution analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Costes' randomization of data did not alter PC-1 to PC-2 or PC-2 to PC-1 overlap in Pkd1 ecKO cells.
source: Costes' randomization of data did not alter PC-1 to PC-2 or PC-2 to PC-1 overlap in Pkd1 ecKO cells.
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data with Costes' randomization analysis.

claim: The mean densities and sizes of PC-1 and PC-2 clusters, PC-2 to PC-1 intercluster distance, PC-1 to PC-2 overlap, and PC-2 to PC-1 overlap were all similar in endothelial cells of Pkd2fl/fl mice and Pkd1fl/fl mice.
source: The mean densities and sizes of PC-1 and PC-2 clusters, PC-2 to PC-1 intercluster distance, PC-1 to PC-2 overlap, and PC-2 to PC-1 overlap were all similar in ECs of Pkd2fl/fl mice and Pkd1fl/fl mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-H and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data comparing Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd1fl/fl cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-H and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: In Pkd2 ecKO cells, PC-1 and PC-2 cluster densities were approximately 12.7% and 11.1% of those in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: In Pkd2 ecKO cells, PC-1 and PC-2 cluster densities were far lower, at ~12.7% and 11.1% of those in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data comparing Pkd2 ecKO and Pkd2fl/fl cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 clusters were smaller and the mean distance from PC-2 clusters to their nearest PC-1 neighbor was far greater in Pkd2 ecKO cells than in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: PC-1 and PC-2 clusters were smaller and the mean distance from PC-2 clusters to their nearest PC-1 neighbor was far greater in Pkd2 ecKO cells than in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C-H).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data comparing Pkd2 ecKO and Pkd2fl/fl cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C-H.

claim: PC-1 to PC-2 and PC-2 to PC-1 overlap were lower in Pkd2 ecKO than Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: PC-1 to PC-2 and PC-2 to PC-1 overlap were also lower in Pkd2 ecKO than Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by SMLM-TIRF imaging data and overlap analysis comparing Pkd2 ecKO and Pkd2fl/fl cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 surface clusters colocalize in endothelial cells.
source: These data demonstrate that PC-1 and PC-2 surface clusters colocalize in ECs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SMLM-TIRF imaging data in both Pkd1fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl cells.

claim: Knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 inhibits the surface expression of both PC-1 and PC-2 proteins, supporting their interdependency.
source: Knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 inhibits the surface expression of both PC-1 and PC-2 proteins, supporting their interdependency.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SMLM-TIRF imaging data showing reduced surface clusters in both Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO cells.

claim: Fluorescent clusters observed in Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO cells appear to represent nonspecific secondary antibody labeling.
source: Fluorescent clusters observed in Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO cells appear to represent nonspecific secondary antibody labeling.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SMLM-TIRF imaging data showing minimal and small clusters in knockout cells.

claim: The inhibition of flow-mediated dilation in Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO arteries is similar to that in arteries of Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO mice when compared to their respective controls.
source: This inhibition of flow-mediated dilation is similar to that in arteries of Pkd1 ecKO and Pkd2 ecKO mice when compared to their respective controls (Figures 2A–C–6C and D and MacKay et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data comparing single and double knockout mice shown in Figures 2A-C, 6C-D, and cited from MacKay et al., 2020.

claim: Lowering bath Na+ concentration inhibited flow-activated ICat in all genotypes and under all conditions.
source: Lowering bath Na+ concentration inhibited flow-activated ICat in all genotypes and under all conditions.
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data showing reduced currents with low Na+ bath solution.

claim: Flow-mediated signaling and vasodilation are similarly attenuated in endothelial cells and arteries of Pkd1 ecKO, Pkd2 ecKO, and Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO mice.
source: When combined with the results of our earlier study, flow-mediated signaling and vasodilation are similarly attenuated in ECs and arteries of Pkd1 ecKO, Pkd2 ecKO, and Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO mice, further strengthening this conclusion (MacKay et al., 2020).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from current study data combined with previous study cited from MacKay et al., 2020.

claim: Inducible, EC-specific knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 similarly inhibits flow-mediated biphasic currents in endothelial cells.
source: Specific results include that inducible, EC-specific knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 similarly inhibits flow-mediated: (1) biphasic currents in ECs, (2) Ca2+ influx-dependent cation currents in ECs, (3) arterial hyperpolarization, (4) vasodilation over a broad shear stress range, and (5) vasodilation that occurs via eNOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from current and previous studies.

claim: Inducible, EC-specific knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 similarly inhibits flow-mediated Ca2+ influx-dependent cation currents in endothelial cells.
source: Specific results include that inducible, EC-specific knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 similarly inhibits flow-mediated: (1) biphasic currents in ECs, (2) Ca2+ influx-dependent cation currents in ECs, (3) arterial hyperpolarization, (4) vasodilation over a broad shear stress range, and (5) vasodilation that occurs via eNOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from current and previous studies.

claim: Inducible, EC-specific knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 similarly inhibits flow-mediated arterial hyperpolarization.
source: Specific results include that inducible, EC-specific knockout of either PC-1 or PC-2 similarly inhibits flow-mediated: (1) biphasic currents in ECs, (2) Ca2+ influx-dependent cation currents in ECs, (3) arterial hyperpolarization, (4) vasodilation over a broad shear stress range, and (5) vasodilation that occurs via eNOS, IK channel, and SK channel activation.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from current and previous studies.

claim: PC-1 knockout elevates blood pressure.
source: We also show that PC-1 knockout elevates blood pressure, consistent with results obtained in Pkd2 ecKO mice (MacKay et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements and consistent with previous study cited from MacKay et al., 2020.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 do not contribute to ACh-induced vasodilation.
source: In contrast, PC-1 and PC-2 do not contribute to ACh-induced vasodilation, indicating that these proteins are activated by specific stimuli and that their knockout does not cause generalized EC dysfunction.
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data showing similar ACh-induced vasodilation in control and knockout mice.

claim: Myogenic tone, depolarization-induced constriction, and passive diameter are similar in Pkd1 ecKO, Pkd2 ecKO, Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO, and control mouse arteries.
source: Myogenic tone, depolarization-induced constriction, and passive diameter are also similar in Pkd1 ecKO, Pkd2 ecKO, Pkd1/Pkd2 ecKO, and control mouse arteries, illustrating that smooth muscle function is not altered in these knockout mice.
evidence: Supported by pressurized artery myography data showing no differences in these parameters.

claim: Flow-activated PC-1/PC-2-mediated stimulation of eNOS, IK channels, and SK channels produces arterial hyperpolarization, reducing the activity of voltage-dependent (CaV1.2) channels in smooth muscle cells.
source: Our data support the following signaling mechanism. Flow-activated PC-1/PC-2-mediated stimulation of eNOS, IK channels, and SK channels produces arterial hyperpolarization, reducing the activity of voltage-dependent (CaV1.2) channels in smooth muscle cells (Garland et al., 2011).
evidence: Proposed signaling mechanism based on experimental data and cited knowledge from Garland et al., 2011.

claim: The reduction in intracellular Ca2+ concentration in smooth muscle cells produces vasodilation and a decrease in blood pressure.
source: The subsequent reduction in intracellular Ca2+ concentration in smooth muscle cells produces vasodilation and a decrease in blood pressure (Jaggar et al., 2000).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental data and cited knowledge from Jaggar et al., 2000.
